title: The Frog Who Went to the Sky

pages.text: In the land of Angola, there lived a young man named Kimana. When it was time for him to marry, his father named many fine young women. Kimana shook his head at each. “I shall marry the daughter of the Sun and the Moon,” he said, “or I shall marry no one.” His father stared. “How will you even ask? Who can go up to the sky?” Kimana wrote a letter asking for the daughter’s hand. Then he went looking for someone to carry it. He asked Antelope. “I cannot go to the sky,” said Antelope.

Kimana shook his head at each.

“How will you even ask?
Who can go up to the sky?” Kimana wrote a letter asking for the daughter’s hand.
Then he went looking for someone to carry it.
He asked Antelope.
“I cannot go to the sky,” said Antelope.
pages.alt: A young man holding a folded letter, looking up at the sun, with his father shaking his head beside him.

pages.text: He asked Hawk. “I can fly high,” said Hawk, “but not as high as that.” He asked Vulture, who flies highest of all. “I can go halfway,” said Vulture, “and no further.” Kimana put the letter away. He was walking sadly by the well when a small voice spoke from the mud. “Give me the letter. I will take it.” It was Frog. Kimana almost laughed. “Those with wings have failed. How can you, who can only hop?” “That is my affair,” said Frog. “Only give it to me.” Kimana had nothing to lose, so he handed over the letter.

pages.alt: A hawk and a vulture looking down from a tree as a small frog speaks from the edge of a well.

pages.text: Now Frog knew something that the others did not. Every day, the water carriers of the Sun and the Moon came down from the sky on a thread spun by Spider. They filled their jugs at this very well and went up again. Frog put the letter in his mouth, slipped into the well, and waited. Down came the young women. One dipped her jug into the water, and Frog swam inside it. She lifted the jug onto her head, climbed the thread, and set it down in the house of the Sun.

Every day, the water carriers of the Sun and the Moon came down from the sky on a thread spun by Spider.
They filled their jugs at this very well and went up again.
Frog put the letter in his mouth, slipped into the well, and waited.
Down came the young women.
One dipped her jug into the water, and Frog swam inside it.
She lifted the jug onto her head, climbed the thread, and set it down in the house of the Sun.
pages.alt: Young women climbing down a shining thread from the sky towards a well, where a frog waits in the water.

pages.text: When the room was empty, Frog hopped out, placed the letter on a table, and hid in a corner. The Sun came in and found it. He read: “I, Kimana, a man of the earth, wish to marry your daughter.” The Sun was amazed. “Who brought this?” he asked the water carriers. They did not know. He wrote a reply: “Come yourself, with a proper gift, and we shall see.” He left it on the table. Frog took it in his mouth, climbed into an empty jug, and rode down to the well the next morning.

The Sun came in and found it.
He read: “I, Kimana, a man of the earth, wish to marry your daughter.” The Sun was amazed.
“Who brought this?” he asked the water carriers.
They did not know.
He wrote a reply: “Come yourself, with a proper gift, and we shall see.” He left it on the table.
Frog took it in his mouth, climbed into an empty jug, and rode down to the well the next morning.
pages.alt: A frog placing a letter on a table in a bright room, with the Sun’s glowing figure entering at the door.

pages.text: Kimana could hardly believe it when Frog put the answer in his hand. He sent back a gift of money. Frog carried it up in the jug. The Sun and the Moon were pleased, and they asked for the full marriage gift. Frog carried that as well, a little at a time. Each time, the people of the sky found the gifts on the table and never saw who had brought them. At last the Sun wrote: “We agree. Let the bridegroom send for his bride.” Now came the hardest part. How could the bride come down?

pages.alt: A frog carrying a small bag in his mouth, sitting inside a water jug balanced on a young woman’s head.

pages.text: Frog thought it over. Then he went up once more. He spoke to the Sun and the Moon himself, for the first time. “I am the messenger of Kimana,” he said. “I have come to bring the bride home.” They were astonished to see who their visitor had been. But they kept their word. The bride came down the spider’s thread with the water carriers, and Frog led her from the well to Kimana’s door. There was a great wedding. And the people of Angola still say: do not despise a small helper, for he may know a road that the great ones cannot find.

activities.question: Why did Kimana almost laugh at Frog’s offer?
options: Even the birds with wings had failed, and Frog could only hop
Frog asked for too much money

activities.question: What did Frog know that the others did not?
options: The sky’s water carriers came down to that well every day

activities.question: How did Frog deliver the letter?
options: He threw it into the air
He rode up inside a water jug and left it on a table

activities.question: Apply it: A big problem at school defeats the strongest pupils. A quiet classmate says she has an idea. Using the tale, what should the others do?
options: Ignore her because she is quiet
Listen, because she may know a way that others have missed
Tell her to try harder at sports

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: Kimana decides to marry the daughter of the Sun and the Moon
Antelope, Hawk, and Vulture cannot carry the letter
Frog rides up to the sky in a water jug
Frog carries the reply and the marriage gifts
The bride comes down and the wedding is held
